new_statements.quote: Although we are unable at this point to describe Tomoip stress in great detail, we note that this general pattern of penultimate stress (with exceptions) is not uncommon among the languages of the area. For similar stress patterns in nearby Austronesian languages, see Johnston (1980a, pp. 125, 143) for Mangsing (i.e., Mangseng), Bebeli, Bali (i.e., Uneapa), Bulu, Bola, and Meramera; Johnston (1980b, pp. 256–259) for Nakanai; Van Der Mark (2007, pp. 33–35) for Vinitiri (i.e., Minigir); and Pearson & van den Berg (2008, p. 14) for Lote.
new_statements.citation: Barlow, Russell & Don Killian. 2023. Tomoip phonetics and phonology. Te Reo (Journal of the Linguistic Society of New Zealand) 66(1): 60-96.
new_statements.locator: p. 80, section 5 'Stress and suprasegmental features' (the text layerof); reference entry for Johnston 1980a on p. 94
new_statements.relation_note: For Tomoip the authors find no phonemic tone, non-contrastive stress that generally falls on the penultimate syllable with exceptions, affixes inside and proclitics outside the stress domain. They then state that this penultimate-with-exceptions pattern is common in the area and cite Johnston (1980a, pp. 125, 143) as reporting similar stress patterns for Mangseng, Bebeli, Uneapa, Bulu, Bola and Meramera. For Bebeli this is a secondhand report: the first-hand statement sits in Johnston 1980a: 125 and 143 (print only, SIL Ukarumpa), which nobody in this project has seen.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Secondhand: Bebeli is said (after Johnston 1980a: 125, 143) to have a stress pattern similar to Tomoip's, i.e. word stress generally on the penultimate syllable, with exceptions. No Bebeli data, no statement of the exceptions, no domain details for Bebeli.
new_statements.exceptions: 'penultimate stress (with exceptions)' is the Tomoip characterisation extended by citation to Bebeli; the Bebeli exceptions, if any, are in Johnston 1980a
new_statements.identity_note: SECONDHAND MENTION ONLY. The article is a phonology of Tomoip (tomo1243, East New Britain), not of Bebeli; Bebeli enters in one comparative sentence (p. 80, section 5 'Stress and suprasegmental features') that cites Johnston 1980a pp. 125, 143 for similar stress patterns in the Kimbe Bay Austronesian languages, Bebeli among them, plus two research-history mentions (Salzner's 'Ba'u (possibly Bebeli)', Grace/Dyen's 'Kapore (i.e., Bebeli)'). The Bebeli meant is unambiguously ISO bek: Johnston 1980a is the Kimbe Bay chapter whose SIL archive record (entry 39242) lists Bebeli [bek] among its subject languages.

sources.citation: Sato Hiroko (佐藤寛子). 2023-2027. ベベリ語の文法記述 / Documentation of the Bebeli languages, Papua New Guinea. JSPS KAKENHI 23KJ2233 (Grant-in-Aid for JSPS Fellows, RPD), University of Tokyo. FY2023 and FY2024 research-status reports
sources.note: Grant record, not a description. FY2024 report: the Bebeli grammar (to begin with 'phonetics and phonology') is still being drafted, draft targeted for November of the following year; only research product listed is the 2025 ICLDC talk. So the grammar does not yet exist as a publication.

sources.citation: Chowning, Ann. 1996. Relations among languages of West New Britain: an assessment of recent theories and evidence. In Malcolm Ross (ed.), Studies in Languages of New Britain and New Ireland 1 (Pacific Linguistics C-135), 7-62. Canberra: ANU. hdl:1885/253884

Comparative/classificatory; section 8.3.2 'Bebeli (Banaule, Kapore)' (pp. 36-38) treats subgrouping, pronouns and possessives only; no occurrence of 'stress' or 'accent' in the text. States that 'the phonemic systems of the languages being discussed here are too poorly described' (p. 58).

sources.access_detail: a digital copy (available on request); access check: open copy online; also held in print at Harvard (Widener Library (offsite storage), call number PL6201.R67 1988)
sources.harvard_location: Widener Library (offsite storage), call number PL6201 .R67 1988
sources.note: Nothing for Bebeli. Bebeli (= Kapore; informant Joseph Neki of Banaule, p. 398) appears only in the Arawe/Pasismanua sound-correspondence tables (pp. 161-167) and in pronoun/article examples (5.152, pp. 182-183); the 11 stress/accent hits in the book concern other languages or general conventions.

sources.citation: Chowning, Ann. 1985. Rapid lexical change and aberrant Melanesian languages: Sengseng and its neighbours. In Andrew Pawley & Lois Carrington (eds), Austronesian linguistics at the 15th Pacific Science Congress (Pacific Linguistics C-88), 169-198. Canberra: ANU. hdl:1885/253420
sources.note: Nothing on stress or tone for Bebeli (the only 'Accent' token is the title of PL C-76 in the references). It documents that vowel transcription in all south-west New Britain wordlists is 'highly suspect' in the e-i and o-u ranges (Johnston 1983: 24) and that Johnston 1980b tentatively set up seven vowel phonemes for Bebeli.

sources.citation: Chowning, Ann. 1978. Comparative grammars of five New Britain languages. In S. A. Wurm & Lois Carrington (eds.), Second International Conference on Austronesian Linguistics: Proceedings (Pacific Linguistics C-61), 1129-1157. Canberra: ANU. hdl:1885/253194
sources.note: No phonology of Banaule/Bebeli at all (morphosyntax comparisons only; the three 'stress' tokens in the text concern Tolai/Rickard 1889 and the verb 'to stress'). Useful only as the pointer to Goodenough's unpublished 1954 Banaule manuscript (sample sentences), the earliest grammatical data on the language.

sources.citation: Chowning, Ann. 1976. Austronesian languages: New Britain. In S. A. Wurm (ed.), New Guinea area languages and language study, vol. 2: Austronesian languages (Pacific Linguistics C-39), 365-386. Canberra: Australian National University. hdl:1885/253004
sources.note: No statement for Bebeli. The chapter is classificatory; its only prosodic content is Chowning's hedged aside that 'some Whiteman languages' (the group comprising Kapore/Bebeli, the Pasismanua chain and Mangseng) may have phonemic tone — a possibility, unattributed to a specific language, offered as a resemblance to north New Guinea languages. Worth flagging for whoever reads Sato's grammar, but not a catalog statement.

sources.citation: Chowning, Ann. 1976. History of research in Austronesian languages: New Britain. In S. A. Wurm (ed.), New Guinea area languages and language study, vol. 2: Austronesian languages (Pacific Linguistics C-39), 179-195. Canberra: Australian National University. hdl:1885/252995
sources.note: No phonology content for Kapore/Bebeli. The chapter is a history of research: it names who collected Kapore material (Goodenough 1961a comparative lists; mission usage 'Bau' for Kapore; Dyen 1965 list too short), and remarks that Kapore speakers are bilingual in Lakalai and have borrowed Lakalai words 'complete with fossilised affixes' (p. 191). The only 'stress' tokens are the verb ('Goodenough particularly stressed the ties..'); 'phonology' occurs only about Friederici 1912 (Barriai) and Counts 1969 (Kaliai-Kove).

sources.citation: Chowning, Ann. 1969. The Austronesian languages of New Britain. In A. Capell, A. Chowning & S. A. Wurm, Papers in Linguistics of Melanesia No. 2 (Pacific Linguistics A-21), 17-45. Canberra: ANU. hdl:1885/145143
sources.note: Nothing: lexicostatistical classification, locations, migration traditions and Lakalai loans in Kapore; no sound-system remarks for Kapore (the stress/tone sentence at PL A-21 line ~351 belongs to Capell's separate paper in the same volume, on other languages).

sources.citation: Goodenough, Ward H. 1961. Migrations implied by relationships of New Britain dialects to Central Pacific languages. Journal of the Polynesian Society 70(1): 112-126.
